title: Shinnecock Monument
summary: The Shinnecock Monument is an economic development project launched in early May 2019. The Shinnecock Nation's goal with this project is to generate revenue to provide for its people. Being a sovereign nation, The Shinnecock Nation maintains the right to build on its land and pursue commerce free from civil regulatory restrictions improperly imposed by New York State.

why_this_matters: Launched in 2019, the Shinnecock Monument represents a major economic development initiative built directly on sovereign tribal territory, despite aggressive regulatory pushback and lawsuits from New York State. This ongoing political battle highlights that the fight for Indigenous self-determination is a modern reality, proving that Native nations continue to actively exercise their inherent right to pursue economic survival on their own terms.

What is a respectful way to visit the Shinnecock Monument and learn from the history it marks?

The Shinnecock Monument consists of two electronic signs along Sunrise Highway in Hampton Bays. Viewed from the public highway, they represent a Shinnecock-led economic development project and a visible assertion of sovereignty.

The Shinnecock Monument refers to two electronic signs installed along Sunrise Highway beginning in 2019 as a Shinnecock Indian Nation economic development project. In May 2020, a New York State Supreme Court decision declined to issue the preliminary injunction sought against the signs; that ruling addressed the request for preliminary relief on the record before the court rather than finally resolving every land-status question. Visitors can learn from the monument while remaining on public roads and respecting Westwoods as private Shinnecock land. Do not enter the surrounding property or treat it as a roadside attraction. The monument connects present-day economic self-determination with a much longer history of Shinnecock land defense.

Sources

  • Shinnecock Nation / Kelly Dennis, Shinnecock Land Claim Historical and Legal Timeline (2018), p. 6.
  • Commissioner of the New York State Department of Transportation v. Polite, 2020 NY Slip Op 50610(U) (May 18, 2020).
